#8122. Ty Burrell Has Some Advice For Parents of Teens

America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.

Let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen. He’s just that kind of guy — disarmingly affable and sincere and funny. This is a good thing because right now he’s talking about meningitis. Yes, meningitis, that overlooked infection that, you probably didn’t know, kills 1 in 10 who develop it with 1 in 5 having long-term health consequences like brain damage and hearing loss. Also, kids age 16 to 23 have the highest rates of it. And that’s what brings us here with Burrell, a dad of two teens, and a message. In partnership with GSK (for the Ask2BSure campaign) Burrell has teamed up once again with Julie Bowen and a stand-in teen actor (mom and dad are back!) to give awareness and, yes, make jokes.

Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!)

So … Why are you, Ty Burrell, America’s dad, talking about meningitis?

Well, it's pretty organic, actually. I have teenage girls, and unfortunately, the most vulnerable population is, actually, I guess, teens to college, 16 to 23. And that's doing large part to the teen lifestyle. My girls play sports, and there's a lot of water bottle swapping. And once you're in college, it's dorm rooms and it's kissing and all of it. And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

But meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. So that's why I'm partnering with GSK on the Ask2BSure campaign to raise awareness about meningococcal disease or meningitis.

To that end, we made a video that we hope is funny, kind of a lighthearted way to educate people and inform people.

It is funny! But I must say as a parent of a 14-year-old, I almost couldn't get the humor because I got afraid.

Yeah, I know. It's a tightrope walk, isn't It?

I happened to have a doctor check in with my 14-year-old this week and I asked them about meningitis. It turns out that I'm two years early. So I'm wondering outside of this PSA, which I think will get people asking doctors, what basic things should parents of teens know.

Well, I would direct them to a healthcare professional in terms of all of the basics. But what I know is that the vaccines available, in terms of strains, A, B, C, W, and Y, but a lot of teens don't have the meningitis B vaccination. And that was true of my 16-year-old. And I did the same thing. When I started to learn more about how serious this was, I had a conversation with our doctor and she hadn't had B yet, so that's now scheduled. And I mean, as far as my knowledge about it, it would be that and really just encouraging people to have a conversation with their doctor about the risks of meningitis and about vaccination, and if that's an option.

It is that simple. I was wondering, I mean, we dads, are always look for a way to make something into a lecture... Is there a way to segue from the meningitis talk or explanation to other necessary talks?

You do have to say it's because you're probably going to be making out with people.

Yeah, totally. I don't know what it's like for you, but I feel like the window in which I actually have any influence for them is three sentences. And I don't know if that's a lack of attention span because of phones or screens or what have you, or it's just time-honored parenting, that you just have the floor for a brief moment before you are tuned out.

“This very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy.”

Totally. And get frustrated fast. It's a lecture. We're now in a lecture. So I don't know about the segueing into a separate topic, but I will say that my wife, luckily, with girls is taking the conversation off of my plate.

Oh great. You can just tell them how dirty dorm rooms are.

That's the dad's role. So you have two teens now. What's the toughest things you've found about raising them and maybe what's the best?

I think that the really natural want for independence, especially our 16-year-old ... Well, actually both of them, we have a 16 and a 14-year-old, but I think they are both craving more independence and more of their own choices and more of their own time. And yet we're still on the job. We are the ones that have to keep them healthy and safe. And so I feel like, I don't know if you feel this way, but I feel like the challenge is really making them feel heard and seen and giving them as much freedom as I possibly can. And still, which it's hard to do because once they experience some of that freedom, it's very hard for them to then have you say, "But not this thing, that's dangerous," or, "That's unhealthy," or whatever that is.

This is why, and this is very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy. I really want to be their friend, but you really can't ... It's not always an option. It just isn't always an option. A lot of points, you have to actually say, "No, you are going to be mad at me, but this is about health and safety." That's the hardest thing. And then I think added on to that, it's like how do you remain connected to them in a time when they're trying to find their own voice and trying to separate from you really? And I think that's completely natural. They are actually trying to pull away so they can be their own selves, and yet it's really important, I think, that you stay connected. I got really good advice from this book a long time ago called The Wonder of Girls, and his advice was like, "They're going to be really mean to you, and don't take it personally." He said, "Just stay nearby. Don't take it personally, be nearby." And that's always been in the back of my mind.

Metaphorically, I'm kind of by the doorjamb of the room. Are you thirsty? Everything okay in there? You safe? But yeah, it's not easy.

That's Great. The Go the F*ck to Sleep author just wrote an essay for Fatherly for his latest book Go to the F*ck to College ...

It just came out! It should be very pertinent to you. But he talks about one piece advice he got from a friend was all teens are saying, "F*ck you, tuck me in. " And I think it's just a more crude way of saying what you were just saying

It kind of covers it. I still get requests. My daughter will act like she never wants to see me again, and then I'll hear like, "Are you not tucking me in? " Okay, I guess there's something there still.

So what's the best part of raising a teen? For the preteen parents in our audience, can you give them some hope — and maybe advice?

I would say the level of nuance in conversation is a real high for me, especially somebody who is interested in comedy. My 16-year-old is pretty stoic. I always think of her as the leading man in a Western or something. She's this person staring off distance, and she's got three words for any answer. But my 14-year-old has always had a strong sense of irony, always, always been funny, and always had a real sense of looking at the world and seeing irony. And as she gets older, her perspective on things, it's pretty remarkable to be around a kid who is starting to see the world and seeing some of the contradictions of the world and some of the things that are unfair, but also just the things that are inherently funny about how seriously we all take ourselves. It's pretty cool. So I think that's one of the great trade-offs is that you end up actually having an intimate relationship with somebody who is really experiencing some of these perspectives for the first time.

That's great. And then any advice for our younger audience? I mean, as far as parenting advice, but also you were thinking about meningitis, any just really pragmatic pitfalls that you would've done differently?

I would say if I were going to go back and re-parent, I would say, "Bend, don't break." I would've given them both more of a leash. Leash is a terrible word for kids really, but you know what I mean? More slack in terms of just they're really exploring who they are and letting them really ... I think we did our best with that, but you're so worried about health and safety, that is mental health, physical health. I think that's a big part of why the meningitis, this campaign to talk about it is really important to me because at the very end of the day, that is the bottom line. No matter whether they consider me a friend or not, I do have to keep them safe. And we've already had lots of bugs go through the family from their interactions with other teens, including mono and all kinds of stuff. But if you get meningitis, that's a whole different ballgame.

Victoria and David Beckham’s tree uses golden-yellow bows instead of loads of ornaments. Experts explain how to copy it, from lights to bow spacing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bows are back and trending for Christmas 2026, as has been well and truly proven by Victoria and David Beckham.

Like trees, candy canes, and presents, bows are about as Christmassy as it gets. It’s the finishing touch on a really sparkly gift, the detail that truly brings out the beauty of a wreath or garlands, and it’s what makes a mantel look dressed for the holiday season.

On a Christmas tree, though? Why, it’s a very simple addition, but it can often prove itself to be the finishing touch that brings the whole thing to life.

Bows are popping up as the go-to Christmas tree ornament all over the place, from garden centers and social media, and it's all down to the likes of Kate Hudson and a whole host of other celebrities... including David and Victoria.

That's right; last Christmas saw the Beckhams decorate their traditional tree with golden-yellow bows rather than a massive collection of ornaments, and shared the results to Instagram.

Swipe to the second slide on the post below to check it out:

A post shared by Victoria Beckham (@victoriabeckham)

The vibe? Why, classy and unique (much as you'd expect from the stylish pair). It’s also way easier to copy than it looks, but it's important to remember that there are a few places where bow-trimmed trees tend do go wrong.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

To help you get it right, we consulted the pros. Here's what they had to say.

When trying to recreate the Beckhams' Christmas tree, most people start with the ribbon, which is a big mistake.

“Buy your lights before you buy your ribbon,” says Nadi Melam, founder and lead preservation artist at Florals Memories, who works with matching color to light. A golden-yellow bow can look orange once the tree is lit. “Warm light bulbs will add orange to anything they touch. Cool-white ones will remove any yellow.”

Interior designer Irena Cara, co-founder of Nova Wrap, recommends warm white as a general rule: “Use warm white lights and place them deep in the tree. Avoid tinsel and multicolored lights as they detract from the ribbon.”

Don't forget to do a test first. “Hold a strip of ribbon up to your lights before buying a full spool,” says Melam. “The wrong spool is your most expensive error.”

The key word here is restraint, and it’s what gives a bow tree like David and Victoria Beckham's tree that expertly designed look.

“Bows look planned when you select one ribbon color and one width,” says Melam. “You end up with too many choices if you use too many colors and widths. That’s what makes a tree look cluttered.”

Cara adds texture to the plan: “Velvet ribbon adds a nice textured element to a tree. Grosgrain and wired satin ribbon keep their shape and can also add nice detail to the tree.” Her limit is “no more than two finishes on the tree.”

While some Christmas trees look great with one oversized ribbon as per the above, those who want to emulate the Beckhams' Christmas tree need to get working on a few more bows than that.

In fact, Cara has a number in mind: “A tree is finished with 20 to 30 bows. They should be spaced about an arm’s length apart and staggered so they don’t form a straight line across the tree.”

Depth matters as much as spacing. “Place each bow deep within the tree, so the branches will embrace it,” says Melam. “If the bow is on the end of a branch, it will droop and move in the breeze.”

Cara’s main warning is about scale: “Decorating too small is the biggest faux pas. Tiny ornaments and thin ribbon get lost on a large tree.”

Do you ever feel completely satisfied when you decorate your Christmas tree only to get comfy on the sofa and realize you missed an entire side of it? “Look at your tree from all sides before you consider it finished,” says Melam.

Cara agrees: “A tree without decorations in the back and bottom of the tree looks unfinished.”

If the tree looks thin in places, definitely don’t make the mistake of adding more ornaments. “Add small evergreen sprigs into any gaps you see before you fill in more ornaments,” says Melam. “You create subtlety by making fewer design decisions and repeating those choices.”

Cara is clear that she’s a designer rather than a horticulturist, but she has noticed which trees hold up well. “The branches of a Fir, such as a Fraser or Nordmann, will keep an even shape and hold the needles better.”

A bow-led tree also helps the branches. “Heavier ornaments and a lot of ornaments on the tree cause the branches to break and bend over time, so place fewer, larger, and more considered ornaments on the tree.”

If you’re trying to be budget-conscious, bows are also a great idea as they’re a lot cheaper than a full set of ornaments. “Using a large, wide ribbon to make bows is cheaper than buying ornaments,” says Cara.

Melam’s advice is to put the money where it shows: “Spend on lights and high-quality ribbon, then use what you have to finish the job.” If you grow your own, she adds, “You can also use dried clippings from your garden as filler.”

Victoria and David Beckham don’t need a cluttered, crowded tree to make a big impression, and neither do you. Just pick the right lights, add a few golden ribbons, and you can get the same polished look in no time flat!

Sarah is a lifestyle and entertainment writer with over a decade of experience covering everything from celebrity news to home and style trends. Her work has appeared in outlets including Bustle, The Everygirl, Hello Giggles, and Woman’s Day. #8120. New York's New AI Law Prohibits Bots From Dangerous Behaviors With Minors

Starting in January, New Yorkers can file complaints with the attorney general if chatbots cross a line with their kids.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere now. It has become part of most Americans’ work and personal lives at an unprecedented pace, popping up in our inboxes and social media apps even when we haven’t opted into a chatbot ourselves. Examples of the harm have rolled in, from staggering numbers of deepfake nudes being created of children to teens who turn to AI for advice during a mental health crisis. But in New York, new legislation will try to rein in the technology and the risks it poses to minors.

The new law, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, prohibits companies with AI chatbots “from offering unsafe features to minors, including chatbots that pretend to be human, build emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage in sexually explicit conversations.” Companies would have to block these features on the accounts of anyone under 18, or any user whose age has not been verified. The law requires chatbot providers to verify users through multiple age assurance methods.

Once verified, that age information must be deleted. It was signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 28, 2026.

According to Gov. Hochul’s website, the legislation prohibits AI chatbots from, among other things:

Violations of the new law could result in fines of up to $25,000 per infraction. The attorney general will publish a new website where New Yorkers can file complaints. New York’s new law is an attempt to curtail the behaviors that are most harmful to kids, experts say.

The story of Adam Raine — a teenager who died by suicide, and whose conversations with ChatGPT exposed that it offered to write his suicide note for him — is one example of why humanizing chatbot behaviors like these are targeted by this law. Surveys have shown kids ages 11 to 16 can’t really articulate what AI is, and many ascribe human-like consciousness and emotions to chatbots.

According to a 2026 Common Sense Media report, nearly 9 in 10 kids ages 9 to 17 (86%) interact with AI, including about one in four who use it on a daily basis. More than half of kids (57%) who use AI said they’ve used it to get information about their health or body; separate studies have found that AI gives misleading or inaccurate health information to users 50% of the time. Half of the respondents have asked AI for advice on decisions about their future or goals, while 37% have used chatbots to discuss their feelings or personal problems.

As always, legislation lumbers along while technology speeds ahead unchecked. Until the laws catch up to AI, parents can feel alone in the fight to protect their kids. Fraser says this law on its own is not enough to protect them either.

“Legislation alone cannot guarantee safety. Companies have got to do their part, and there has got to be accountability,” she says. “The Meta settlements are a great example of what industry self-regulation looks like. It doesn’t work. There’s got to be third-party independent accountability because companies, for all sorts of reasons, can’t always take five steps back to see what it is that they’re doing. Sometimes they can't see the risks that are right in front of them. So I do think that the law is a step in the right direction. We need these types of laws, but we also need the companies to do their part.”

As New York readies to enforce its new youth AI protections, just this week Google, Meta, and TikTok filed a lawsuit against the state of California, challenging its legislation prohibiting addictive social media features on children’s accounts. The law bans the platforms from offering “psychologically exploitative features” to minors, including autoplay videos, endless scroll, and personalized recommendations that contribute to “compulsive use.” The companies argue the government is trying to impose its judgment over parents'.

This article was originally published on November 5, 2026

#8119. Dr. Becky Kennedy on self-trust, boundaries and letting kids struggle

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 30, 2026

Dr. Becky Kennedy’s daughter once wrote home from summer camp asking for more bikinis, including one from a pricey brand her friends had. By their phone call a few days later, she didn’t care about any of it. For Kennedy, a clinical psychologist and the founder of Good Inside, that exchange says a lot about raising confident kids at a time when parents can fix almost any discomfort with a tap. She defines confidence as self-trust, built in the hard moments we’re most tempted to smooth over. In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Kennedy opens up about the two jobs every parent has, why “I just want my kid to be happy” falls short and how to support a struggling kid with one foot in and one foot out.

Meet the expert: Dr. Becky Kennedy is a clinical psychologist, the founder and CEO of Good Inside and the author of three New York Times bestsellers. Known to millions of parents simply as Dr. Becky, she teaches an approach built on two core parenting jobs, holding boundaries and validating feelings, and on the idea that kids grow confident by getting through hard moments with support. With Carter’s, she recently launched the Childhood Confidence Project, a free program for parents. A Duke graduate, she lives in New York City with her husband and their three kids.

Dr. Becky Kennedy: I don’t ever assume I have the right answer. This might sound weird. I’m not that attached to the right answer. I’m very attached to having a way to think through problems, and it makes me think about the difference in the question “What do I do? What am I gonna say?” versus “What’s really going on here? What’s my job?” Those are very different questions. I think confidence as a parent for me comes from having a repeatable way to think through hard moments. I think the thing that takes away from our confidence as parents is in every hard moment with our kid, we feel like we’re starting over. And I think that’s the thing that gives me confidence, is not knowing I can handle any situation well, but feeling like I can think through it.

Dr. Becky Kennedy: I think a parent has two jobs, almost always. One job is to set boundaries. It’s the piece that we’re missing in modern-day parenting. We’ve over-corrected. Boundaries are decisions I make with my kid that almost inherently they don’t like today but are actually good for the type of person they need to become tomorrow. And boundaries are things we tell our kid we will do, and they require our kid to do nothing. We often think we’re setting a boundary when we’re actually making a request. “Please stop jumping on the couch. Don’t hit your brother.” Those are requests. Those are not boundaries. A boundary is an assertion of my very appropriate authority. The other part of our job is staying connected to our kids and validating their feelings, which doesn’t mean agreeing, which doesn’t mean letting their feelings dictate our behavior. But just seeing their feelings as real. Those two jobs answer, I think, kids’ questions that they’re always unconsciously asking. Am I safe and am I real?

Dr. Becky Kennedy: I don’t think confidence is feeling good about yourself all the time. I think confidence is self-trust. I always tell parents it’s actually not feeling like the best. It’s trusting it’s okay to be you when you’re not the best, ironically. So was I the kind of kid going through childhood who trusted myself, who felt like I was okay being me even when something was really hard? No. I was a really perfectionistic kid. I was a kid who probably growing up had enough external success, good grades, A team in soccer, all that, that I could use external outcomes as a way of feeling good. We know it works sometimes in childhood, and then it catches up to you and crashes big time. When we think about kids who are so just oriented towards success, in a way, we’re setting them up to have a shrinking life. I want my kids to have a wide range of situations. I want them to say, “Yeah, I’m trying out for that team. Sure, I might not make it, but let’s see.” That’s confidence.

Dr. Becky Kennedy: This might sound funny. It has never been easier as a parent to make our kids’ life easier. And I think that is the biggest problem we have with confidence and resilience. You see someone have something, it’s a natural human urge to be like, “I need that right away.” We are doing such an insane disservice to our kids by pairing what happens to be the peak urge with the ability to get the thing in the moment. I saw this with my own daughter. She was away for a little bit in the summer. She wrote me a handwritten letter. “I don’t have enough bikinis. Could you send me two of the ones I left at home?” And then she said, “And a lot of my friends have this brand. Maybe it’s too expensive, but I would love one of those.” I knew I was talking to her in a couple days. At the end of the call, I said, “Hey, by the way, you haven’t brought up bikinis.” This is what she says: “Oh, yeah, I don’t need those. It’s fine.” I can’t even tell you what this did for me in my parenting. Just having time allowed her urge and her panic to subside that she didn’t even care. And because it’s never been easier to remove those things, it has never been harder to raise an actually capable, confident, resilient kid.

Dr. Becky Kennedy: People will say this in passing. We’re talking about our kids at a dinner and someone’s like, “I just want my kid to be happy.” And I’m sure my husband always looks at me like, “Just don’t. Please, just let this pass.” And sometimes I do, but sometimes I’m like, “No, we don’t.” I don’t think our job is to make our kids happy. I actually would say that if you’re operating even unconsciously as if that is your job, you’re setting your kid up not for happiness, but, if I say it as directly as I think it, you’re setting your kid up for a ton of anxiety and fragility. Because so much of capability in adulthood comes from the range of situations we learned to handle in childhood. Three of my best friends were in the same class in second grade, and I wasn’t. Now, do I think when my kid is 40, they’re gonna be thinking about who’s in their class? 0%. But it’s not about the class, it’s about the circuit. And you know what’s gonna happen when I’m 40? I’m gonna see a group of moms at lunch without me. I’m gonna see a group of people at work get promoted before me. We have to be able to handle jealousy and sadness and being left out for there to be room for happy.

Dr. Becky Kennedy: I just wanna zone in on that moment, your kid gets a zero, because again, we tend to think in extremes. No part of me thinks you should be in that car ride being like, “Sucks. Yep, zero sucks. Yep, figure it out.” There’s just a lot between that. And it’s interesting, the phrase, “I don’t want you to worry about that.” I think what we’re trying to say is, “I don’t want you to take this moment and feel like that’s just defined who you are.” But I do want you to worry a little. When our kid is in a hard situation, you don’t wanna leave them alone, and you don’t wanna fully jump in. I think you want one foot in and one foot out. One foot in would be saying, “Ugh, you weren’t expecting that. You didn’t want that to happen. Well, that’s a bummer on this Thursday car ride.” Whatever’s just the truth. And the one foot out is sometimes words, and it’s usually after some time, which is, “All right. This is recoverable. One number doesn’t change anything about you. You’re the same smart, awesome, responsible kid before the zero as you were after the zero.”

Dr. Becky Kennedy: Think about tummy time. Tummy time is one of the first times your baby is telling you, “Me no likey.” My job isn’t to remove all moments of discomfort for my baby. Now again, we go to the other extreme. “Oh, so you’re saying you just leave a baby crying?” No, I would never do that. But we’ve started to confuse, at all ages, giving comfort with making kids comfortable. They’re completely different things. My job is to provide comfort. My job is not to always make my kid comfortable. Okay, I’m gonna do tummy time. My baby might whine a little bit, cry a little bit. I’m gonna get next to my baby. “Oh, you’re right. This is hard. Oh, you’d rather be on your back. Oh, you know what? We’re gonna do 10 more seconds together, and I am right here with you. I know you can do it. You are doing it. Oh, you did it. I’m giving you a big hug. You did something so tricky.”

Dr. Becky Kennedy: The scripts are helpful to talk about because ideas that are theoretical aren’t that usable. But where scripts are limiting is, I’m not a script person. I really mean that. I saw a comment, she goes, “Me and my husband, in any hard situation, look at each other and we say WWDBD.” What would Dr. Becky do? Now, the reason I love that is completely different than why I think people would think I love it. This actually has nothing to do with me. If you’re in a hard situation and you say, “What would Dr. Becky do?” That’s not my voice. I’m literally not there with you. That is your voice. Having a method, having a way of thinking through something. And that, to me, more than a perfect script, that is the most confidence-building thing as a parent.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Listen to the full conversation on the Motherly Podcast.

#8118. The Cool Dad’s Guide to Father’s Day

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow)

But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also shows how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it."

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”

Then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

Llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a big role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas says, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”

Tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”

Llamas says he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in New York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”

This Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”

#8116. Tiffani Amber Thiessen Talks Parenting Teens, Period Talks & Her Witchy Era

The “Saved By The Bell” alum has come full circle and is now playing a principal and mom.

Tiffani Amber Thiessen’s face is burned into the brains of every elder Millennial who watched countless Saved by the Bell episodes and dreamed of dressing exactly like Kelly Kapowski. Of course, we’ve all left the 1900s behind and have grown into adults — parents and women with careers.

Like the rest of us, the 52-year-old mom of two kids — Harper, 16, and Holt, 11 — has left high school in the rear view mirror, but her career continues to flourish. And she’s still in the classroom, in a way: Coven Academy, the witchy dark academia series in which she stars as the principal of Crescent Veil Academy, just got renewed for a second season.

You can also find her on Instagram, where her account is a delightful mix of food, fashion, humor, nostalgia, and life as a woman who is finding power and peace as she enters her 50s.

Recently, Thiessen partnered with Always on its “Period Talks Don’t Have to Be Scary” campaign, which addresses what is often a real hurdle for parents: talking about periods with their kids. Research has found that 43% of moms struggle to start the first-period talk because they feel unprepared. So Thiessen wants to share her own experiences while offering practical advice to parents who want to open and informative with their tweens and teens... even if can be awkward at times.

She recently sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about periods, parenting, her new show, and her family’s holiday traditions.

Scary Mommy: Gen Z and Millennial moms have done a lot to break period stigma with our kids. How have you done that with your kids?

Tiffani Amber Thiessen: I think the generation I grew up in didn’t talk about these things. Now kids are much more open, and I have a very open relationship with both my children. It never fully takes away the scariness of intimate talks, whether it’s periods, the body, or growing up. But I think parents who understand that it isn’t one big, intimidating conversation, but many small, casual talks, can take the edge off.

Partnering with Always has been lovely because they’re trying to prepare parents with what to do and how to have that first conversation. Being prepared gives you the confidence.

SM: I found that I was a lot more scared than my daughter was. Did you feel that?

TAT: Most parents feel that way. You don’t realize until afterward that it really isn’t that scary. I found it to be a bonding moment. I’d tell my kids that over half the population menstruates, so it’s not a big deal. Keeping it casual and a little funny helps. Building that competence between parent and child is what lets your daughter take it on, and it’s a badge of honor.

SM: I love asking this: What’s your best piece of parenting advice?

TAT: It goes back to having an open conversation about anything. When I became a parent, I wanted to be open to receiving anything my kids share, whether it’s hard or difficult. I wanted them to feel comfortable and know I would never judge. We’ve all been in crazy places, and my kids are super open with me, about the fun stuff and the stuff that isn’t so fun. Keeping that conversation free of judgment is probably the most important thing in parenting.

SM: Have you ever wanted to judge, though?

TAT: I can secretly judge, is that okay? [laughs]

TAT: Most of the things my kids tell me I’ve either witnessed, been through, or know someone who has. It’s really not that crazy.

SM: Let’s switch gears to Coven Academy. And you just got renewed for Season 2?

TAT: Monday! We had high hopes and wanted to find an audience that saw the specialness of the show, and I think we did. It’s done very well on Disney+ and Hulu, so we’re over the moon to do it all over again.

SM: There are so few shows made for this demographic: tweens, mostly girls. It’s so good to have something that speaks to kids in that space.

TAT: The witch aspect is having a moment on social media, but it’s not really about spells and potions. It’s about found family, sisterhood, and having each other’s backs. I have a teenage daughter, and she has a wonderful group of girls she can count on. Everybody should have that, especially women.

SM: How has it been going from being a student on a hugely popular show to a headmistress on set with the younger generation?

TAT: It feels natural. I have kids of my own now. The last few shows I’ve been fortunate to do have had younger casts, and I really enjoy working with young adults. I may give them advice, but I get a lot from them, too. We did a lot of night shoots, and I’d see these kids at 3 a.m. doing their TikToks while I was struggling. Their energy kept me going through those nights.

SM: The holidays are coming up. Do you have any family traditions you want to share?

TAT: We’re very traditional in that it’s all about family. We do Christmas morning and Christmas Eve dinner. For the last 15 or 16 years, we’ve alternated between my husband’s family in Texas and ours. This year it’s our turn to go to Texas. We leave the day after Christmas and spend the week and New Year’s with my in-laws. All the cousins are together, and we look forward to it every year.

SM: What have you been cooking lately, or what are you planning for the holidays?

TAT: My kids like the traditions. Thanksgiving is classic turkey and stuffing, plus my mom’s famous cream cheese pie. For Christmas we usually do enchiladas, which I’ll probably make again this year. We usually switch it up for Christmas because everybody’s over turkey.

SM: Dennis Haskins recently passed away. He was your principal on Saved by the Bell, and now you’re playing a principal. Do you have any remembrances to share?

TAT: I have so many. He was our solid one; our anchor. I know it was probably hard for him, being the only adult on a kids’ show. He handled it with such grace and gave us a safe place. He was part of us, and he could be young, but he was still a strong personality. He always made us feel protected, and he’s very much missed.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#8115. 35 Back-To-School Sports Gear Essentials Every Young Athlete Needs

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

Back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

Most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and big enough to get them through practice.

The 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

Some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

This variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

Some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. A protein bar is useful before practice, after practice, or between games, but check school rules and allergens before tossing one into a team bag.

This 10-count variety pack has flavors built around chocolate, peanut butter, blueberry, fruit, and nuts. The bars are gluten-free, made with simple ingredients, and have 12 grams of protein per bar, but some contain common allergens including eggs, peanuts, almonds, and cashews.

Fall sports still mean sun exposure. A sweat-resistant sunscreen belongs in every sports bag, especially for after-school practices, weekend tournaments and kids who swear they “don’t burn.”

This sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

This has a spacious main compartment for school and practice gear, plus a ventilated shoe compartment to keep wet sneakers or cleats away from clean clothes and tech. The water-resistant base is the quiet win here, because locker room floors, wet fields, and rainy parking lots are not kind to regular backpacks.

Wet socks, damp towels, and postpractice clothes should not touch anything clean. A wet-dry bag keeps the gross stuff contained until someone remembers laundry exists.

These bags are technically built for diapers, swimsuits, and day care messes, which is exactly why it works for youth sports. The 12.5-by-16-inch size, washable fabric, heat-sealed seams, and leak-resistant design make it useful for wet socks, damp towels, and gear you do not want touching anything else.

Cotton is fine until it turns into a wet dish towel with sleeves. A moisture-wicking shirt helps kids stay more comfortable through practice, conditioning, and the ride home.

The quick-drying fabric wicks sweat and dries fast, which is the whole point of a practice shirt. It is soft enough for school or general wear too, so it does not become another piece of gear that only gets used once a week.

Every young athlete needs shorts that can handle sweat, dirt, turf, and repeated washing. They should be light, easy to move in, and not so expensive that losing one pair becomes a family event.

The listing calls these soccer shorts, but the sweat-wicking Climacool fabric, adjustable drawcord waist, and recycled polyester interlock make them useful for more than one sport. They are built for movement and repeated washing, which is what matters.

Bad underwear can ruin a practice faster than bad weather. Athletic underwear should move, breathe, and stay put under uniforms, shorts, and base layers without bunching, pinching, or becoming the thing your kid complains about the entire ride home.

These have a 5-inch inseam, a wide soft waistband, a breathable athletic feel, and flatlock seams for durability. The contoured pouch and tagless back make them a practical under-uniform option for boys who need support without bulk.

These are made with smooth stretch fabric, a seamless waistband, and a tag-free design to help reduce irritation during school, sports, and everyday movement. The lightweight performance fabric gives active kids a flexible fit without pinching, digging, or bunching under gear.

A hoodie is the unofficial uniform of kids waiting before games, riding home after practice, or denying they are cold.

This is a straightforward school-to-practice hoodie with a relaxed fit, kangaroo pocket, thumbholes, and midweight fabric. It is the kind of layer kids can wear constantly without making you nervous every time it leaves the house.

A base layer helps with sweat, coverage, and comfort without adding bulk. It works under jerseys, hoodies, and uniforms when the weather cannot decide to be seasonally appropriate.

This long-sleeve top is made with lightweight HeatGear fabric that wicks sweat and dries fast, with mesh panels for ventilation and flatlock seams for easier movement. It is not a heavy thermal layer, but that is why it works for school sports: Kids can wear it under gear without overheating five minutes into warm-ups.

Socks disappear faster than almost anything else in a young athlete’s life. Buy more than seems reasonable, because wet, thin, or blister-making socks can wreck a practice fast.

These socks use a combed cotton and polyester blend with spandex for stretch, which means they are built to breathe, hold their shape, and survive repeated washing. The medium cushioning and reinforced heels and toes make them a practical everyday pick for kids who burn through socks like it is part of the sport.

Slides give kids something easy to wear before and after games, especially when cleats are muddy, socks are wet, or feet need a break. They also make locker rooms, pools, and postpractice errands less gross.

These slides use OOfoam, which the brand says absorbs 37% more impact than traditional footwear foams. The closed-cell foam is machine-washable and designed to minimize odor, which makes it perfect for locker rooms, postgame errands, and the ride home.

A quick-dry towel works for sweat, rain, swimming, muddy legs, and the towel situation no parent wants to inspect. It dries faster than a regular bath towel, which matters when it gets forgotten in a bag overnight.

The listing says it absorbs five times its own weight and dries fast when hung by the snap loop. It also packs into a ventilated carry bag, which makes it easier to keep in a sports bag than a bulky bath towel from home.

A sports bag becomes a swamp fast. Packing cubes give clean clothes, extra socks, base layers, and small gear a fighting chance of staying together instead of becoming part of the bottom-of-the-bag sludge.

These packing cubes keep clean backup clothes, socks, and small gear organized inside a sports bag, backpack or a duffel. The Del Dia colors are random and one-of-a-kind, which means no two sets look the same, and your kid has a chance — albeit small — of recognizing their own stuff.

Youth sports shoes can turn toxic fast, especially when they live in a bag between practices. A shoe deodorizer helps keep sneakers, cleats, and slides from stinking up the car, mudroom, or whatever corner your kid has claimed for gear.

These compact deodorizers are built for shoes, gym bags, lockers, and sports gear, so they do not just solve one stink problem. The twist-to-activate design lets kids control the scent level, assuming they remember to use these before the shoes become a family issue.

Some sports smells do not come out in the wash because the offending item never goes in the wash. A gear spray helps with helmets, gloves, pads, bags, and other equipment that gets sweaty, rank, and somehow keeps getting used.

This spray deodorizes sports equipment, including helmets, gloves, bags, pads and gym gear, and the brand says it works for everything from football and hockey to lacrosse, soccer, volleyball, and boxing. It only requires a spray-and-air-dry routine, which is about as much cleaning as most sports families can promise on a weeknight.

Keep one in the sports bag, one at home, and maybe one in the car, because youth sports have a way of exposing every deodorant failure.

This deodorant is dermatologically tested and made for young, sensitive skin, which makes sense for kids who are just starting to need it. It is designed to protect against body odor without using a grown-up scent that announces itself from across the room.

Sometimes there is no shower. Body wipes help kids clean up enough to survive the car ride, dinner, homework or whatever comes next.

These individually wrapped 8-by-10-inch wipes are made for the exact no-shower problem sports families know well. They are hypoallergenic, paraben-free, and alcohol-free, and include aloe vera and vitamin E, so they are a practical bag staple for postpractice cleanup.

Fields, gyms, locker rooms, and portable bathrooms are not exactly sterile environments. Hand sanitizer is small, cheap, and useful before snacks, after bathroom runs, and after handling shared gear.

This unscented trio gives you three travel-friendly sanitizer sprays, which is useful if you want one for the sports bag, one for the car, and one that will disappear immediately.

Sunscreen, deodorant, lip balm, wipes, hair ties, and sanitizer should not be rolling loose at the bottom of a sports bag. A small toiletry bag keeps the tiny essentials together and makes them easier to find

This zip pouch has internal mesh pockets and a separate compartment, so the small stuff has a fighting chance of staying organized. The swivel hook is useful for hanging it in a locker, on a backpack or anywhere that is not the bottom of a filthy sports bag.

Lips burn too, and kids almost never think about it. SPF lip balm is small enough to live in a bag and useful for long days outside.

This three-pack has SPF 30 and includes aloe and vitamin E to help protect and moisturize lips. The multi-pack is useful because lip balm has the life expectancy of a loose sock.

Late-summer and fall practices can come with mosquitoes, especially on fields near grass, water, or woods. Bug spray keeps kids from spending half of practice swatting instead of playing.

This spray repels mosquitoes, ticks, and biting flies, and the misting design gives more even coverage than the panic-spray method most kids use.

Hair ties vanish, break, and somehow become community property. Keep extras in the sports bag for any kid who needs hair out of their face, whether they play rec soccer or want to look like Norway’s Erling Haaland before warm-ups.

These hair ties are designed to flex with different hair thicknesses and hold without pinching or pulling. They are also made to minimize breakage, which matters when a kid is ripping out a ponytail in the car after practice.

Fall sports do not stop because the weather is annoying. A lightweight rain jacket gives kids real coverage for wet practices, sidelines, and the long walk from field to car.

This waterproof nylon shell is light enough to layer but protective enough for everything from drizzle to a sudden downpour. It has a hood, two hand pockets, elastic cuffs, and reflective detail, which makes it a practical all-season piece for kids who will absolutely claim they are fine while visibly getting soaked.

Something will hurt. A reusable ice pack is useful for bumps, sore knees, rolled ankles, and the ride home after a hard practice.

These reusable gel packs stay flexible out of the freezer, so they can wrap around knees, ankles and other hard-to-ice spots. The included soft cover adds a barrier between the cold pack and skin, which makes it easier to use in the car or on the couch after practice.

Reusable ice packs only help if someone remembered the freezer. Instant cold packs belong in a sports bag or tournament kit for away games and minor sideline injuries.

These single-use cold packs activate after folding, so parents do not need a freezer, cooler, or advance planning to get cold therapy on the sideline. They are designed to reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit, which is exactly the point.

Athletic tape is the thing nobody thinks about until someone needs it immediately. It can help with sore knees, cranky ankles, tight shoulders and small body complaints that show up five minutes before warmups.

This 16-foot roll can be cut to size, so parents are not locked into one strip length for every kid, joint, or complaint. It is breathable, hypoallergenic, and latex-free, and it’s designed to stay on for one to three days through sweat, showers, and weather, while still allowing a range of motion.

New shoes, wet socks, and long tournament days can turn a small hot spot into a full limp. Blister bandages take up almost no room and can save a practice, game or long ride home.

These hydrocolloid bandages cushion blisters, cuts, and scrapes while helping protect them from water, dirt and germs. They are waterproof and designed to stay on for up to five days, which is useful when a kid’s heel is already angry and the season has no interest in pausing.

Youth sports produces scrapes, turf burns, mystery cuts, and dramatic reactions to minor blood. A small first-aid kit should have bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and the basics you need before anyone starts searching the glove compartment for a napkin.

This compact hardcase packs 120 supplies, including adhesive bandages, butterfly closures, gauze pads, alcohol prep pads, antiseptic wipes, sting relief pads, gloves, tweezers, scissors, and medical tape. It is slim enough to fit in a backpack, glove box, or sports bag, but stocked well enough for the everyday cuts, scrapes, and minor injuries that come with kids playing hard.

This is the most sport-specific item on the list. It matters for football, lacrosse, field hockey, basketball, martial arts, wrestling, and other sports in which player contact, falls, elbows, or sticks can impact teeth.

This boil-and-bite mouthguard molds to the teeth for a more custom fit and is made with shock-absorbing EVA material to help protect teeth, gums, and jaw during contact sports. The slim profile, airflow vents, and optional strap version make it more practical for kids who need protection but still have to breathe, talk, and keep it in place.

If it is not labeled, it is a donation to the lost-and-found economy. Name labels help water bottles, hoodies, towels, bags, shoes, and gear make their way back before another parent takes home the same black sweatshirt.

This 114-label pack includes stick-on clothing labels, shoe labels, large and small rectangle labels, and bag tags, so parents can mark almost everything that leaves the house. The labels are peel-and-stick, waterproof and laundry-safe, which matters when the gear is sweaty, wet, washed constantly, or lost somewhere between the field and the car.

Long practices, races, meets, and tournament days can turn kids into empty tanks fast. Energy chews are quick, portable fuel for older kids who need carbs they can eat fast without digging through a bag for whatever got crushed at the bottom.

These chews have 23 grams of carbs per serving. They are organic, include sodium to help replenish electrolytes after exercise, and are easier to stash in a gym bag than a full-size snack.

Warm-up pants used to mean joggers, but kids have moved on. Wide-leg sweatpants are the more current version: loose; comfortable; and useful before practice, after practice, or on the ride home.

These have an elastic waist, pockets, and a wide-leg cut that feels more current than basic warm-ups. The fabric is lightweight, soft, breathable, and slightly stretchy, which makes these useful for school, practice, running around, and the postgame outfit change your kid suddenly cares about.

These have a straight, wide-leg cut, letter print, and loose, trendy fit that works with hoodies, jackets and sweatshirts. They are made for daily wear, workouts, sports, running, and outdoor activities, which puts them in the exact lane between warm-up pants and “my kid will actually wear these.”

This is not performance gear. This is for the kid who walks off the field sweaty, red-faced, and suddenly needs to fix their hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot.

This sea salt spray is made to add volume, shine, and gritty texture without the crunch. It adds grip before styling, which should help with the sacred ritual of fixing the hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot. Postgame vanity is real, and frankly, it may be the most consistent part of youth sports.

#8114. I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

Home / Relationships / Marriage & Partnerships

Here's how I reclaimed my time without compromising care for my little ones.

By Lais de Oliveira Updated Nov. 05, 2026

Every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and announces he’s going out for something spontaneous. Lunch with a friend. A bike ride. He’s gone in about ninety seconds if I don’t stop him at the door.

And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.

Standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it? Not once since my first child was born… three and a half years ago. Then it hits me: I am the proverbial default parent.

In my life, I have moved countries on 48 hours’ notice. I have started businesses and communities on four continents, landed in cities where I knew no one, and figured it out from the ground. Yet here I am, unable to walk out my own front door without a negotiation.

Now I am the kind of person who books a haircut six weeks out.

My husband carries himself with the lightness of someone who isn’t carrying the majority of the parenting load.

The mental one: how many diapers, ounces of milk, and clothing changes need to be packed for a single outing. The emotional one: forecasting ways to address my little one’s growing feelings or managing the conditions to prevent a meltdown. The logistical one: managing energy levels and knowing a missed nap isn’t worth the spontaneity of welcoming last-minute visitors (the hosting of which, by the way, would fall on me).

He doesn’t carry any of that because I do. And I know I’m not alone in this. (There are even several Bluey episodes about it).

But I thought my husband and I would be different. And to his credit, he does a lot for the family, and has always been willing to work towards a situation where I felt supported. Still, for over three years, our day-to-day behaviors set our sails in a different direction; the mere idea that we were working toward a mostly equitable deal blinded me to the fact that, too stereotypically, I was the one carrying the invisible load of parenting.

For a while, I stewed silently, filing away every every “just tell me what to do” and every unplanned walk out the door.

But my resentment wasn’t getting me closer to the future I actually wanted, which is to raise my kids alongside a partner I trust. Anger is honest information, but a terrible operating system. It costs you the very thing you’re angry about losing: your own energy.

So I stopped waiting for space to appear and started claiming it. Here are the steps I took:

The first step was recognizing there was a real problem. Only then could I have a productive, fact-based conversation with my husband.

What helped: talking it out, sharing the situation with friends and watching them nod before I finished the sentence. Those conversations helped clear the fog and made it clear: I had become the default parent without ever applying for the role, and I needed it recognized as a real job, with real requirements, not something invisible and easily taken for granted.

Clarity is a prerequisite for being heard, and it is what moved the conversations with my husband past defensiveness. Until then, the idea that we had a “mostly equitable deal” was blurring his perspective too.

We didn’t get it right at once. Several conversations left one of us hurt, misunderstood, or underappreciated. But we persisted in having the difficult ones. Those conversations eventually gave us enough clarity to lay out, with clinical precision, the ways our partnership had been uneven. We could dissect a messy situation and turn resentment into discernment, naming the areas where I was lacking support and the areas where both of us were lacking appreciation.

Clarity let us stand across from each other, our vision for an equitable partnership leading the way instead of resentment for how it had been.

And we learned something more important: an equitable relationship isn’t found. It’s built. That shared understanding made the next steps possible.

Once we both understood what my resentment had been trying to say, in more positive, proactive terms, my needs became clearer and easier to ask for. And my husband finally had something concrete to act on.

We put our partnership to work: I defined clear steps to reclaim my own freedom, and he redefined what it means to be a supportive partner.

From there, we made a real plan: a family calendar that protects my time the same way it protects his and provides a predictable rhythm. The gym, daily. Tango on Monday nights. A weekday or two blocked out because I’m in the city for meetings. An evening for dinner with a friend.

And, every so often, a half-day on the weekend for my own creative retreat, which is where I am as I type this: in a literal room of my own, my office and studio, with a door that closes.

I still won’t leave the house on a whim. But neither will he. We plan ahead, tell the other person, and arrange childcare if we both want some time out.

Relationships tarnish under unmanaged resentment. Bringing back the shine takes work.

From my end, I had to listen more, or proactively ask for his perspective on an issue I’d raised, and work to transmute resentment into something more productive: naming my unmet need. I had to really care about his perspective, and trust that he had been going for “supportive partner” all along, even if our early attempts had been clumsy and left scars.

From his end, he needed to become more observant and make efforts to show up more often in ways that were meaningful to me: offering to hire help for things previously expected to come from me, checking in before making plans on his own, and looping me in before inviting friends and family.

We also started scheduling more romance, whether a babysitter-powered date or quality time at home. But I’d say this came as a consequence of everything above: there was no mood for a date while our relationship was permeated by resentment. The difficult conversations had to come first.

The work most mothers do is largely invisible. But invisible isn’t the same as involuntary.

I can’t undo how the default got set, or how my own behavior kept reinforcing it. What I can do is refuse to let the default compromise my own health, my relationship, and the example I’m setting for my children. I want them to have the courage to create a life they’re proud to call theirs.

Some of that courage looks like walking out your own front door on a Saturday, keys in hand, for no reason at all: knowing the little ones are safe, and well cared for, because you made it so.

#8113. Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

The second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

“Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

According to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”

It’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

This article was originally published on November 6, 2026

#8112. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

When Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He shows Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

But the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.
